newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says hopes for early solution on EMU pact.
newsitem.headline: France says hopes for early solution on EMU pact.

text.p: France's finance minister said on Wednesday the government wanted an early solution to the dispute over an EU budget pact but insisted it must win its demand for a greater focus on growth and jobs before it signs up to any deal.

Analysts said Paris was signalling a willingness in principle to approve the pact at an EU summit in Amsterdam next week provided France can drive a hard bargain in making unemployment the top priority in Europe.

"We are clearly going to find a solution. If we can move forward quickly, it is obviously better. No one wants to drag things out for the sake of it," Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said after the weekly cabinet meeting.
"The question is to know how we can obtain the balance we are seeking," he told reporters.

France's new Socialist-led government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary victory on June 1, is seeking a better balance in Europe between budget discipline and price control on one hand and growth and jobs on the other.

At a finance ministers' meeting in Luxembourg on Monday it withheld approval of the "stability pact" limiting the budget deficits of countries that join a single European currency, stunning EU partners who then rushed to say they too had always seen jobs as a priority.

Strauss-Kahn has said France is simply trying to enforce the 1991 Maastricht Treaty which calls for greater economic policy coordination among European countries and stresses growth and jobs alongside fiscal discipline and price control.
"Let's apply the treaty and not just 10 percent of the treaty," a source close to prime minister Lionel Jospin said.
"The French government merely wants to respect the spirit and letter of the treaty," former European Commission president Jacques Delors, an adviser to Jospin, said this week.

The government is trying to restore a balance reached between Paris and Bonn when the treaty was negotiated in the early 1990s, which it fears has been lost in a German-dominated approach in recent years.

Germany has always emphasised the need for an independent central bank, guaranteeing price and currency stability. France has pushed for a more political vision stressing the need for economic growth to boost employment.
In arguing its case, the government is also trying to fulfil campaign pledges to turn Europe away from austerity and win support for France's call for a European "economic government".
Faced with a very tight EU timetable -- with the Amsterdam summit deadline fixed before it came to power -- it is trying to turn the shortage of time to its advantage.
"We are trying to capitalise on this momentum to get a number of things through, given that all our partners know they have to negotiate," a government source said.

"I'm sure the government would like to reach an agreement this weekend," UBS economist Darren Williams said. "But obviously they are not going to sacrifice all their election pledges just to come up with an agreement on time."
Jospin has declined comment on whether he would sign up to the stability pact at the Amsterdam summit, which he will attend alongside President Jacques Chirac.

But Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said after talks in Paris on Tuesday that Jospin had told him he did not need to wait until he made his policy speech to parliament on June 19. That lifted one major potential obstacle to a deal in Amsterdam.
What remains is the language of a declaration -- which could either be added to the stability pact or made as a separate "growth pact" stressing the need for growth and jobs.
Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, has been charged with trying to work out the wording with his EU colleagues.
French and German leaders and ministers will also be at a summit meeting on Friday in Poitiers, western France, for further talks on Europe and the stability pact.
